Cheap food and bad food overlap a lot less than you'd think.

The trick is telling them apart before you order. 3 rules:

1. A short menu is a good sign.

A taqueria selling four things buys those four ingredients in bulk and wastes nothing. That's why it's cheap.

A cheap 60-item menu is getting there some other way, and you can usually taste it.

2. Go at lunch.

The same kitchen often charges a lot less at lunch for nearly the same plate. Lunch specials and set menus are the most reliable way to eat somewhere good on a small budget.

3. Ignore the $ signs.

Price bands average the whole menu. A "$$" place can have a $9 lunch plate, and a "$" place might only be cheap if you eat sides.

Look up the price of one filling dish instead.

Where the value usually hides: taquerias, pho shops, halal plates, dosa, banh mi, rice plates.

Cheap because they specialize, not because they cut corners.

The full guide: https://www.savorscout.net/what-to-eat/on-a-budget

Food tastes like nothing when you have a cold, and it's not the kitchen's fault.

Most of what you call taste is really smell. Block your nose and you're down to five things: salt, sweet, sour, bitter and heat.

Heat is the useful one. Chili isn't a taste at all, it's a pain signal, and it gets through a stuffy nose just fine. So does sour.

That's why hot, sour, salty food still lands when you're sick, and a subtle dish tastes like warm nothing.

So when you're sick, order:

• Tom yum
• Hot and sour soup
• Pho with extra lime and chili
• Congee with pickles

And lean on steam. There's a reason almost every culture's sick-day food is a soup.
Not a cure, just food you can actually taste. More on eating when you're sick: https://www.savorscout.net/what-to-eat/sick-with-a-cold

"Where do you want to eat?" gets silence. "Is Thai okay?" gets an answer in two seconds.

That's the whole trick to deciding where to eat. 3 ways to use it:

1. Name the sensation, not the cuisine.

"Something crispy and spicy" narrows the field faster than "Asian food," and it's easier to answer honestly. A cuisine is a category. A craving is a constraint.

2. Let something else make the first cut.

Reacting to one concrete suggestion is much easier than coming up with one from nothing. If it's wrong, you'll know instantly, and you'll know why.

3. In a group, veto instead of vote.

Ask five people to name a place and you get five answers. Ask them each to remove the one thing they won't eat and you have a shortlist in one round.

And skip the star ratings. A 4.6 taqueria and a 4.6 steakhouse aren't comparable, and neither number knows you're tired and want something sour.

More: https://www.savorscout.net/what-to-eat/cant-decide

It's dark at 5 now, so here's the cold-night rule:

Only leave the dorm for food that's better in a restaurant than at home. Hotpot. Korean BBQ. Ramen. Birria. A curry somebody started four hours ago.

Best sign you picked right: the windows are fogged up from the inside.

And on a cold night, close beats best. The good place five minutes away wins over the great one twenty minutes away.

What's your fogged-window spot near campus?
The whole cold-night guide: https://www.savorscout.net/what-to-eat/cold-rainy-night

For whoever's coughing in the back of lecture: food tastes like nothing when you're congested because most of taste is actually smell.

What still gets through is salt, sour, and chili heat, since heat is a pain signal, not a taste.

So order tom yum, hot and sour soup, pho with extra lime and chili, or congee with pickles.

Not a cure, just food you can taste. Send this to the sick friend.
More on eating when you're sick: https://www.savorscout.net/what-to-eat/sick-with-a-cold

Midterm-week dinner advice that sounds fake but isn't:

When you're stressed, the menu matters more than the food. A 60-item menu is genuinely worse tonight, because reading it is work.

Pick somewhere with a short menu, food that comes out fast, and no wait. Or somewhere you already know. Trying a new place costs attention you don't have right now.

What's your no-thinking-required spot?
The full guide to eating when you're stressed: https://www.savorscout.net/what-to-eat/stressed
